overview.text: Confucianism is a Chinese ethical and philosophical tradition shaped by teachings associated with Confucius (c. 551–479 BCE) and generations of later thinkers. Its texts do not present one unchanging doctrine: the Analects preserves selected sayings and episodes, while later writers developed and reinterpreted Confucian ideas. Central themes include learning and moral self-cultivation, humaneness (ren), ritual propriety (li), and responsibilities within relationships. Filial piety—care and respect toward parents and ancestors—serves as a starting point for wider ethical conduct. Confucian ideals influenced education, government, and social life in China and spread into broader East Asian intellectual traditions.

key_facts.text: Confucius is conventionally dated to c. 551–479 BCE; the tradition associated with him developed through later followers and interpreters.
The Analects collects sayings and accounts of Confucius’s actions; it is not a single, unified treatise presenting fixed doctrines.
Humaneness (ren), ritual propriety (li), learning, and moral self-cultivation are important themes in Confucian thought.
Filial piety connects conduct toward parents and ancestors with broader responsibilities; Confucian texts also relate family duties to public roles.
Confucian teachings became influential in Chinese education and government, including the training of officials, and later interpretations spread across East Asia.
